channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] A brake controller safety recall quietly fixed a wirelessly reachable code execution flaw
item.description: Researchers at the National Motor Freight Traffic Association found that a 2024 safety recall for the Bendix EC80 heavy-vehicle brake controller also silently fixed serious security defects, alongside the memory corruption issue Bendix publicly disclosed. The researcher identified buffer-handling flaws that could crash the electronic control unit and enable remote code execution, a hardcoded password capable of disabling traction control, and a further path to both a crash and code execution. Three vehicle makers integrating the EC80 issued recalls covering an estimated 450,000 units. The vulnerabilities could be reached through wireless signal injection onto the J2497 powerline databus or through compromised connected devices such as trailer telematics. The EC80 handles anti-lock braking, traction control and stability functions, so the affected component is a safety controller rather than an infotainment or telematics box. - NMFTA research — reported by SecurityWeek and Truck News - Research published 7 Aug 2026; recalls issued late 2024

item.title: [High] Treasury names an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network operating inside US critical infrastructure
item.description: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, within a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels. Five alleged operators, described as tied to the Mabna Institute, were indicted by the Justice Department the preceding week. Treasury says the network has been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. The scope is worth reading precisely: what is attributed here is espionage and data theft, not manipulation of process equipment. The State Department has posted a $10 million reward on related activity. Transportation is not among the sectors Treasury names, and rail operators should not read this as a warning aimed at them specifically. The relevance is structural. The access paths described — stolen credentials, compromised IT service providers and remote-management footholds — are the same routes that reach a railroad or transit agency through a signalling vendor’s support tunnel, a dispatch software supplier, or a shared state or municipal identity system. Espionage-grade access is disruption-capable access held by someone with different orders. The second consequence is regulatory and practical: TSA security directives already require covered railroad and transit owner-operators to report cybersecurity incidents to CISA, and sanctions designations change the legal calculus around any extortion payment decision. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; Department of Justice indictment; State Department Rewards for Justice notice — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop and Nextgov/FCW - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers on exposed networks
item.description: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build custom tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software. Those tools give read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over the S7comm protocol. Critical manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities are named as the most-targeted sectors. Actors locate exposed or poorly segmented devices with internet scanning services and get in through default or weakly configured credentials rather than exploiting a vulnerability. Affected lines run from the S7-200 and S7-300 through the S7-1200 and S7-1500, including F-series safety controllers. Rail is not named, but S7-class controllers are widespread in station and depot building services, platform screen door interfaces, escalator and lift control, tunnel ventilation, yard and washplant systems, and wayside auxiliary equipment — much of it commissioned by contractors and connected for remote support. - Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Issued 19 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] North Carolina Ports intrusion disrupts cargo processing at a rail-served inland port
item.description: The North Carolina State Ports Authority detected an unauthorised intrusion on 4 August that triggered a systems-wide IT outage affecting processing workflows across all three of its facilities: the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the rail-served Charlotte Inland Port. Truck movements, cargo processing and administrative systems were disrupted while restoration was underway, though terminal operations and vessel activity continued and some cargo processing shifted to manual handling. No control system was involved. For railroads and intermodal operators the significance is that inland port throughput is a shared dependency: a partner’s outage constrains rail movements and dwell without any part of the railroad’s own network being touched, and most operators have no contractual visibility into how long that partner expects recovery to take. - North Carolina State Ports Authority — reported by Cybernews and Splash247 - Detected 4 Aug 2026; reporting through Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s red team took a domain undetected — the tooling was fine, the monitoring was not
item.description: CISA published AA26-237A on 25 August comparing two red-team assessments run with near-identical tradecraft: one against a government services and facilities organisation, one against a water and wastewater systems entity. Both opened with phishing and escalated through Active Directory weaknesses that are ordinary rather than exotic — a Machine Account Quota left at its default of 10, and misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services templates. The outcomes diverged sharply. At the organisation CISA labels A, the team obtained elevated domain privileges and reached sensitive business systems and cloud resources without ever being detected, despite the organisation running multiple security operations centres and multiple EDR products. CISA’s stated reason deserves reading twice: the SOCs did not communicate with one another, and thousands of false positives from routine business activity buried the real signal. Railroads and transit agencies should read the second finding first. The corporate Active Directory this tradecraft targets is commonly the same directory that authenticates dispatch workstations, CAD/AVL clients, maintenance-of-way systems and the back-office servers supporting positive train control — and at transit agencies it is frequently a shared municipal or state domain the agency does not itself administer. Both weaknesses named cost nothing to fix. The detection failure is the one that maps onto this sector: monitoring split between agency IT, a city SOC and a signalling integrator is exactly the uncorrelated multi-console arrangement CISA describes. - CISA cybersecurity advisory AA26-237A — joint red-team assessment findings - Published 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Six agencies warn the Gunra ransomware crew is walking into critical infrastructure through two 2025 Fortinet bugs
item.description: CISA, the FBI, the Defense Cyber Crime Center, the NSA, the Secret Service and the Korean National Police Agency published joint advisory AA26-222A on 10 August on Gunra, a ransomware operation that has hit organisations across critical infrastructure sectors since April 2025. The advisory’s operational point is unglamorous: Gunra’s initial access is overwhelmingly through internet-facing edge devices, and specifically two Fortinet flaws — CVE-2024-21762 and CVE-2024-55591 — both patched in 2025 and both still reachable on unpatched appliances. Once inside, the group steals data before encrypting, and runs a double-extortion leak site. The agencies published detection guidance, indicators and a set of mitigations centred on patching edge appliances, enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and segmenting recovery infrastructure. Passenger and freight operators are in the critical-infrastructure set this advisory covers, and the entry point is a perimeter appliance rather than anything rail-specific. The operational risk for rail is the same one Pittsburgh Regional Transit lived through: lose the business and asset-tracking systems and you lose the ability to see where stock is, even when signalling itself is untouched. - CISA / FBI / DC3 / NSA / USSS / ROK National Police joint advisory AA26-222A — reported by The Record and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Industrial ransomware up 12 percent in Q2, disrupting operations without control-system access
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents involving industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1,020 in the first quarter, with manufacturing taking 747, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The finding that transfers to rail and transit concerns mechanism rather than sector counts: disrupting the IT systems that support an operation is frequently enough to interrupt it even when attackers never reach the control system, and extortion continued shifting from encryption toward data theft. For a passenger operator the equivalent systems are ticketing, real-time passenger information, crew rostering and paratransit scheduling — several of which carry statutory service obligations. For a freight railroad they are waybill, yard management, crew calling and customer portals, none of which stops a train but all of which stop a business. - Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A conferencing server was made to hand out a backdoored client to the engineers who joined the call
item.category: Threat intel — Supply chain / engineering workstations
item.description: Kaspersky ICS-CERT reported on 12 August that the Head Mare group chained two flaws in unpatched TrueConf Server installations — tracked by Kaspersky as KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058 — to run code and escalate privileges on the server, then swapped the legitimate client installer for a trojanised build carrying the PhantomCore and PhantomGraph backdoors. Anyone who subsequently updated their conferencing client from that server was infected. The victims named span instrumentation, electronics, transportation, energy, IT and software development. TrueConf shipped fixes on 18 June 2026 for versions 5.3.x before 5.3.9, 5.4.x before 5.4.9 and 5.5.x before 5.5.5; the exploited servers were simply never updated. Transportation is one of the sectors Kaspersky names. Railways run a large conferencing estate across operations control centres, maintenance depots, signalling contractors and rolling-stock suppliers, and the people on those calls are frequently the same ones holding signalling engineering tools and remote-access credentials into wayside and depot systems. A backdoored client distributed as a normal update crosses straight into that population. - Kaspersky ICS-CERT — corroborated by The Hacker News and SC Media - Published 12 Aug 2026; patches released 18 Jun 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA sets a three-day federal deadline on a CVSS 10.0 Oracle web-tier flaw now under active attack
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-21962 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 24 August with a remediation date of 27 August — the tightest window Binding Operational Directive 26-04 permits. The flaw is an improper access control issue in Oracle HTTP Server and in the Oracle WebLogic Server Proxy Plug-in for Apache HTTP Server and Microsoft IIS, scored CVSS 10.0. It is reachable over HTTP by an unauthenticated attacker with no user interaction and no existing privileges, and successful exploitation allows access to the instance or modification of the data it fronts. Oracle shipped the fix in its January 2026 critical patch update; reporting on 25 August describes broad exploitation against WebLogic servers. A three-day federal deadline is the signal worth reading — CISA reserves that window for exploitation it judges both live and consequential. This is not an ICS product and it will not be trackside, but Oracle’s web tier is a common reverse proxy in front of the systems a railroad or transit agency runs on: ticketing and fare portals, customer information feeds, asset and maintenance management, crew scheduling, and the reporting layers that pull operational data out of dispatch and PTC back-office systems. Ukrzaliznytsia’s ticketing outage is a reminder that passenger operations degrade visibly long before anything trackside is touched. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition; Oracle critical patch update — corroborated by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Added to KEV 24 Aug 2026; federal remediation deadline 27 Aug 2026; Oracle fix issued Jan 2026; broad exploitation reported 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
item.description: Citrix published bulletin CTX696939 on 20 August covering two NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws. The serious one, CVE-2026-19490, is an authentication bypass carrying a CVSS score of 9.3: on Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations an unauthenticated attacker can skip the login step entirely. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory overflow that can produce unpredictable behaviour or a denial of service, and only applies where SIP ALG is enabled on a Large Scale NAT group. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21 or later. Citrix, Rapid7 and Finland’s national cyber authority all said they were not aware of in-the-wild exploitation at publication, while urging immediate patching — NetScaler has a long record of exploited edge flaws. On a rail estate NetScaler typically fronts supplier access into signalling maintenance networks, depot systems and station equipment, and connects remote control centres. An unauthenticated bypass there matters more than the CVSS number suggests, because that appliance is often the only boundary between a contractor’s laptop and a maintenance VLAN that reaches trackside. - Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Bulletin published 20 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August covering Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager, the software operators use to monitor and manage Simplex fire alarm panels across a property portfolio. Versions up to and including V2.01 keep user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while the application runs, tracked as CVE-2026-27875 and classified as CWE-316. A local attacker who already holds low-privileged access to the workstation can read those credentials out of memory and reuse them against the application and the systems it connects to. CISA lists critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy among the affected sectors, with deployment worldwide. Johnson Controls has published remediation guidance in JCI-PSA-2026-28. Stations, depots and control centres run Simplex fire detection, and on a rail estate the fire-alarm management workstation is almost always a facilities asset — shared account, in a back office, administered by a building services contractor rather than the signalling or IT team. That is precisely the local low-privileged access this flaw needs to yield working panel credentials. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28 - Published 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable service causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, requiring no authentication and no user interaction. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. In rail these appliances typically terminate supplier access into signalling maintenance networks, depot systems and station equipment, and connect remote control centres — so exploitation removes the remote diagnostic path exactly when a fault needs a specialist who is not on site. - Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek - Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS Patch Tuesday: Ruggedcom and Desigo alongside a maximum-severity IoT2050 flaw
item.description: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most severe, SSA-834709, is a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers and high-severity flaws across Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort, with medium-severity issues resolved in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories for NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Three of these are common in rail estates specifically: Ruggedcom switches in trackside, tunnel and substation cabinets, Desigo in station and depot building services, and Siveillance as a station and platform video management platform. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709 and related advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For rail and transit the IKE and vCenter entries carry the most weight. IKE terminates the site-to-site tunnels linking control centres, depots, stations and supplier networks. vCenter often manages the virtual infrastructure hosting SCADA, passenger information and back-office systems, where compromise is a hypervisor-level problem rather than an application one. SharePoint is worth a second look in this sector because signalling design documentation, safety cases and maintenance procedures are so often stored there and classified as ordinary business content. - CISA KEV catalogue additions - Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] TSA rail security directive runs to 15 January 2027 while the surface cyber rule remains proposed
item.description: Security Directive 1580-21-01E, Enhancing Rail Cybersecurity, took effect on 16 January 2026 and runs through 15 January 2027, applying to designated freight railroad carriers and requiring performance-based cybersecurity measures including incident reporting to CISA. Behind it sits the broader rulemaking, Enhancing Surface Cyber Risk Management, which would require higher-risk pipeline, freight railroad, passenger railroad and rail transit owners and operators to establish and maintain a comprehensive cyber risk management programme and report incidents to CISA. That rule remains proposed rather than final, so the directives continue to carry the obligation. The practical planning point is the annual reissue cycle: directives are renewed rather than permanent, and each renewal has historically tightened expectations, so an operator building only to the current text tends to be behind at the next issue. - TSA Security Directive 1580-21-01E and the Enhancing Surface Cyber Risk Management proposed rule - SD 1580-21-01E effective 16 Jan 2026, expires 15 Jan 2027

item.title: [Medium] From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations take effect on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting those products: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure being available, or within a month for a severe incident. Reporting flows through a single reporting platform to the relevant national CSIRT with simultaneous availability to ENISA. The obligations cover products already on the EU market, not only new releases. For rail this cuts two ways. Operators buying signalling, rolling stock systems and station equipment from EU-facing suppliers should expect faster and more formal vulnerability disclosure from September. Operators who themselves place digital products on the EU market are manufacturers under the Act. - European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations - Obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026
